summary: This section explains how long the leaders and members of the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal can stay in office. It sets rules about their age limits, how many terms they can serve, and when they can be appointed. It also mentions that members can keep a right to return to their previous workplace for a short time.
points: The President and members of the Tribunal serve for a term of five years and can be reappointed for one more five-year term.
The President can hold office until age sixty-seven, while other Tribunal members can hold office until age sixty-five.
The chairperson and members of the Appellate Tribunal serve for a term of five years and can be reappointed for another five years.
The Appellate Tribunal chairperson can hold office until age seventy, and other members until age sixty-seven.
A person must be at least fifty years old to be eligible for appointment as a member.
A member may keep their lien with their parent department for a period of up to one year.
example: Mr. Sharma, aged fifty-two, is appointed as a member of the Tribunal starting January first. He looks forward to serving his five-year term. Under the rules, he is eligible to be re-appointed for one more term of five years after this term ends. He will be able to hold office until he reaches the age of sixty-five. Before taking this role, Mr. Sharma worked in a government ministry. He decides to keep his lien with that parent ministry while holding his new office, but this arrangement can last for no longer than one year.

terms.meaning: An official body set up to deal with specific legal matters and disputes.
Being chosen again to hold the same position for another term.
A legal right to hold or keep a position or connection with a previous employer or department.
The main group or department where an official originally worked before taking a new post.

watch: Note that the maximum age limits and terms differ depending on whether the person belongs to the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal.
